title: Interpretability Framework for LLMs in Undergraduate Calculus
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to evaluate large language models (LLMs) in mathematics education beyond simple final-answer accuracy. The authors argue that correctness alone does not capture whether an LLM’s reasoning is reliable, pedagogically sound, or conceptually valid, especially in undergraduate calculus where multistep symbolic reasoning is essential. To address this gap, they propose an interpretability framework designed to analyze how LLMs reason through calculus problems and to identify when apparently fluent solutions are actually conceptually flawed.

The proposed approach has two main components. First, a reasoning flow analysis decomposes LLM-generated solutions into stepwise operations, concepts, and cognitive complexity labels, producing a structured reasoning trace. Second, a prompt sensitivity ablation procedure perturbs parts of the input prompt and measures how much the model’s output changes, using metrics such as robustness, phrase sensitivity, and reasoning complexity. The framework is applied to real Calculus I, II, and III university exams, and the authors also compare baseline zero-shot prompting with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and contextual retrieval setups.

The study context is undergraduate calculus at a U.S. institution, using aggregated class average scores from courses with approximately 50 students each and expert grading by mathematics faculty. The paper also involves educators as evaluators and sources of expert feedback on pedagogical alignment and model limitations. Gemma 3 was selected as the main model after comparison with LLaMA 2 and LLaVA-7B, and its exam responses were benchmarked against student averages across multiple calculus courses and exams.

The main conclusions are that LLMs can perform competitively on some undergraduate calculus assessments, sometimes matching or exceeding average student performance, but they remain brittle and can produce fluent yet conceptually incorrect reasoning. The framework revealed sensitivity to prompt phrasing, weaknesses in conceptual understanding, and cases where retrieval augmentation degraded rather than improved performance. The authors conclude that interpretability tools of this kind are necessary for transparent, responsible deployment of LLMs in STEM education, particularly for tutoring, feedback, and assessment contexts.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's Gemini family large language model used for general-purpose text generation and problem solving.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the primary LLM ('Gemma 3' in the paper text appears to refer to the selected model) to solve undergraduate Calculus I-III exam questions, benchmark against student averages, and analyze reasoning with the proposed interpretability framework, including baseline, RAG, and contextual retrieval conditions.

findings.finding_summary: On course exams, the selected model achieved mixed performance relative to class averages. Reported scores were: Calculus I Exam 1 = 44/70 (62.9%) vs class average 88.8%; Exam 2 = 48/70 (94.2%) vs 82.1%; Final = 74/100 (74.0%) vs 73.0%; Calculus II Exam 1 = 49/60 (80.0%) vs 89.6%; Exam 2 = 52/60 (86.6%) vs 85.2%; Final = 72/90 (80.0%) vs 72.9%; Calculus III Exam 1 = 84/100 (84.0%) vs 78.0%; Exam 2 = 74/100 (74.0%) vs 80.3%; Final = 112/150 (74.6%) vs 71.3%.
findings.measure: Faculty-graded undergraduate calculus exam scores compared with class average percentages

findings.finding_summary: For consistency testing, the model was run five times on the same Calculus I Exam I and received the same mark, reported as 59, across all runs. The paper states outputs were consistent in formatting, solution approach, and mathematical notation usage.
findings.measure: Across-run consistency of graded exam score and output formatting on repeated administration of the same exam

findings.finding_summary: Retrieval augmentation had uneven effects. In Calculus I Exam I, baseline was 62.9%, improving to 70.0% with RAG and 65.7% with contextual retrieval; in Calculus II Exam I, baseline was 80.0%, RAG 81.7%, contextual retrieval 75.0%; in Calculus III Exam II, baseline was 74.0%, but RAG dropped to 52.0% and contextual retrieval to 64.0%, both below the student average of 80.3%.
findings.measure: Faculty-graded exam percentage under baseline, RAG, and contextual retrieval conditions

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA family large language model for general-purpose text generation and problem solving.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated during baseline model selection on Calculus I Exam 1 for mathematical answering quality, consistency, and formatting compliance.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic LLM interpretability framework for analyzing model-generated mathematical reasoning via reasoning-flow decomposition and prompt ablation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper's main contribution is a post-hoc interpretability framework applied to LLM-generated undergraduate calculus solutions to diagnose conceptual flaws, prompt sensitivity, and robustness.

findings.finding_summary: Using the proposed framework on real Calculus I-III exams, the authors report that LLMs often produced syntactically fluent yet conceptually flawed solutions, and that reasoning patterns were sensitive to prompt phrasing and input variation. The paper also reports an example attention/ablation analysis where important prompt elements included '(-1, 4)' with impact 0.630, '∇f' with impact 0.562, and 'directional' with impact 0.477, illustrating sensitivity to specific input components.
findings.measure: Interpretability metrics including phrase sensitivity, robustness, reasoning complexity, and ablation-based impact scores

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark/framework paper using faculty-graded exam comparisons and repeated runs, but it does not report randomized or quasi-experimental causal designs, statistical testing, or full sample-level analytic detail. Evidence is therefore exploratory/descriptive rather than strong causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported impacts are mixed: the selected model sometimes exceeds class averages, sometimes underperforms, and retrieval augmentation can help or substantially hurt depending on exam context. No standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported, so overall impact remains unclear.
